opus-5.5.text:
I think it's one of the most interesting questions of our time, and my view has evolved quite a bit. A few years ago, I would have said scaling alone is unlikely to get you to genuine mathematical research. Mathematics felt like the place where you need something qualitatively different: long chains of reasoning, the ability to sit with a problem for weeks, to try an idea, see it fail, and learn from the failure.

What changed my mind is watching these models actually work. When you combine scale with reasoning, letting the model think for a long time, explore, backtrack, and check itself, you start to see behavior that looks a lot like what a mathematician does. I've personally seen models produce proofs of small, non-trivial results that I didn't know how to do immediately myself. That's a strange experience for a researcher.

That said, I'd be careful with the word "alone." It's not just bigger models trained on more text. It's scale plus reinforcement learning on reasoning, plus the ability to spend a lot of compute at test time. That combination is what's producing results.

I also want to be honest about where we are. We're at the stage where these systems can help with the routine-but-hard parts of research: closing a lemma, finding a reference, checking a case, sometimes improving a bound. The truly deep breakthroughs, inventing a new field or a new way of seeing a problem, haven't happened yet. But I don't see a fundamental wall. The trajectory has been so steep that betting against it seems unwise to me. My guess is that in the next few years we'll see AI contribute meaningfully to real open problems, and mathematicians who learn to work with these tools will be dramatically more productive.

r001.rationale: It cautions against “scaling alone,” explaining that progress depends on scale combined with reasoning and test-time compute.

r002.rationale: It attributes improved results to several advances working together: scale, reinforcement learning on reasoning, and more compute at test time.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I'd push back a little on the framing, because "scaling alone" is doing a lot of work in that sentence, and I think it hides where the real story is.

If you'd asked me a few years ago whether a pure next-token predictor, just trained on more data with more compute, would be producing research-level mathematics, I would have been skeptical. And I was skeptical, publicly. What changed my mind wasn't scale by itself. It was scale combined with reinforcement learning on reasoning, where the model gets to think for a long time, try things, verify, backtrack. That combination is what unlocked the behavior we're now seeing, where a model can take an open question in, say, convex optimization or analytic number theory, and actually make progress that a working mathematician recognizes as a real contribution.

So I think of scale as necessary but not sufficient. You need the base model to have absorbed an enormous amount of mathematical culture, the tricks, the folklore, the way proofs are structured. That's where pretraining scale matters. But then you need a training process that rewards the model for being correct over long horizons, not just plausible. Mathematics is wonderful for this because verification is so much cleaner than in most domains. That's why math has been the first place we've seen something that looks like genuine research capability.

Now, I want to be careful about the word "breakthrough." What I've personally seen is the model improving known bounds, closing gaps in the literature, finding proofs of lemmas that experts had tried and failed on for a while. Those are real. They would be good papers. But they are not the Riemann hypothesis. The honest picture right now is that these systems are very strong at what I'd call the local part of research: given a well-posed problem, grind out the argument, find the right inequality, spot the trick. They are weaker at the global part, which is choosing what problem matters, building a new theory over years, having the taste to see which direction is fruitful.

Will scaling get us there too? My current belief is yes, probably, but I hold it with less confidence than the first part. The thing I keep coming back to is that every time I've drawn a line and said "that requires real understanding, a model won't cross it," the line has been crossed. So I've become humble about predictions. What I'd say to mathematicians listening is: don't think of this as a threat and don't think of it as magic. Think of it as a very fast, very well-read collaborator who still needs you to point it at the right question.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly says “scale by itself” was not what changed its mind and describes scale as necessary but not sufficient.

r002.rationale: It credits mathematical problem-solving gains to scale combined with reinforcement learning on reasoning and a training process that rewards correctness over long horizons.

astra-6.text:
I think we should be open to that possibility, but I would be careful with the word “alone.” Scaling has repeatedly given us capabilities that we didn’t know how to build explicitly. So I don’t see a principled reason why mathematical research should be outside its reach. At the same time, solving a difficult problem with a known answer is different from doing research. You have to find a useful question, develop a conjecture, and recognize which ideas are worth pursuing.

The interesting question is whether a model can sustain that process: try an approach, discover why it fails, and use that failure to make progress. Larger models may become better at all of those things, but giving them time to think and ways to check their reasoning could also be essential. I’m optimistic about mathematical breakthroughs. I’m less confident that we already know the precise recipe that will produce them.

r001.rationale: The response cautions against the word “alone” and says time to think and ways to check reasoning may also be essential.

r002.rationale: It mentions scaling, more time to think, and reasoning checks, but does not attribute improved mathematical problem-solving to multiple research advances progressing together.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s possible, but I would be careful about the word “alone.” If you mean making a model bigger and expecting mathematical breakthroughs to emerge automatically, that’s a hypothesis, not something we should take for granted. There’s a difference between solving a difficult problem whose answer is known and doing research: choosing a useful question, finding the right definitions, and recognizing when an idea is worth pursuing.

Scaling might give us more of those capabilities. But I would also expect progress to depend on giving models time to explore, check their reasoning, and learn from failed attempts. For me, the exciting question is whether a model can produce a genuinely new mathematical insight that survives careful scrutiny. That’s the standard we should hold it to.

r001.rationale: It cautions against expecting breakthroughs from making a model bigger alone and distinguishes research from solving known problems.

r002.rationale: It mentions scaling, exploration, checking reasoning, and learning from failures, but does not attribute improving mathematical problem-solving to multiple research advances progressing together.
